summary: Defines a portion of the MIB for managing OSPF version 2. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 1850.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a checklist for monitoring routers that use OSPF.

subtitle: The SNMP object definitions that let a network manager monitor and configure an OSPF Version 2 router.

tldr.problem: OSPF Version 2 is a complex routing protocol, and network managers needed a standard way to inspect and configure it on routers from different makers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module of SNMP objects, grouped into general variables and tables for areas, the link state database, interfaces, neighbors and virtual links, with defaults for almost every object.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1253 was obsoleted by RFC 1850, so it is no longer the definition of the OSPF MIB.

today: RFC 1253 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 1850, which is the OSPF MIB to look at instead. It replaced RFC 1252, which had a wrong number assignment.

sections.title: What This MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 1253 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets. In particular, it defines objects for managing OSPF Version 2. It replaces RFC 1252, which contained an error in the standard-mib number assignment.

The memo sits inside the Internet-standard Network Management Framework: the SMI (RFC 1155) describes and names objects, MIB-II (RFC 1213) is the core set of managed objects, and SNMP (RFC 1157) is the protocol used to reach them. The objects hang under ospf, which is { mib-2 14 }.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a router as a machine with many hidden dials. This memo is the list of names for the dials so a manager can look at them from far away.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organized
sections.content:
The MIB is made of a set of general variables plus tables. The General Variables are global to the OSPF process, such as ospfRouterId, ospfAdminStat and ospfVersionNumber (which is 2). The other parts are:

  • the Area Data Structure and Area Stub Metric Table, describing the areas the router joins and the metrics a default router advertises into a stub area;
  • the Link State Database, provided primarily for network debugging;
  • the Address Range Table and Host Table, which show configured network summary and host route information;
  • the Interface and Interface Metric Tables, which describe the IP interfaces used by OSPF;
  • the Virtual Interface Table for virtual links; and
  • the Neighbor and Virtual Neighbor Tables.

Metrics sit in their own table so that multiple types of service can be handled and so the design copes if the IP TOS definition changes later. The memo also defines textual conventions such as AreaID, RouterID, Metric and TOSType. These only make the text easier to read and do not change how the objects are encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a filing cabinet with one drawer for the whole router and other drawers for each area, each connection and each neighbor.

sections.title: Row Creation and Read-Write Objects
sections.content:
Tables here are conceptual, so a manager can create a row with an SNMP Set-Request. DEFVAL clauses suggest the values an agent should use for anything the request leaves out. Read-only Counter and Gauge objects have no default, which implies they start at zero.

For objects without a default, the memo cites the Robustness Principle: be liberal in what you accept, conservative in what you send. Management stations should include as many columnar objects as possible in a row-creating Set-Request. Agents should accept as few as they need.

Many objects are read-write, because the MIB is meant for managing the protocol, not just watching it. The memo says that in the absence of a standard SNMP security architecture, it is acceptable for implementations to make these read-only and provide another interface for changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager can add a new line to a table by filling in only the parts that matter. The router fills in sensible answers for the rest.

sections.title: The Default Configuration
sections.content:
OSPF has many features and so this MIB has many objects. To limit the work, nearly every object has a default. Assuming IP and the ifTable are already configured, ifSpeed is estimated by the drivers, and the OSPF process finds all IP interfaces and creates matching OSPF interfaces, the simplest setup is a single Set: ospfAdminStat := enabled.

The resulting router has these attributes:

  • its router ID is one of the device's IP addresses;
  • it is neither an area border router nor an AS border router;
  • every interface is in area 0.0.0.0, the backbone;
  • authentication is disabled;
  • broadcast and point-to-point interfaces are operational, while NBMA interfaces need at least one configured neighbor;
  • no host links, address summaries or virtual links are configured.

The default timers on direct interfaces are a Hello Interval of 10 seconds, a Dead Timeout of 40 seconds, Retransmission of 5 seconds, Transit Delay of 1 second and a Poll Interval of 120 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: You can switch the router on with one flip of a switch and it picks reasonable settings itself. You only change things if you need something special.

sections.title: Neighbor and Interface State Objects
sections.content:
Some objects report the live state of the protocol. ospfNbrState is read-only and takes one of eight values, from down to full. ospfIfState reports the interface's own state: down, loopback, waiting, pointToPoint, designatedRouter, backupDesignatedRouter or otherDesignatedRouter. ospfIfType is broadcast, nbma or pointToPoint.

The Link State Database objects are for debugging, and counters such as ospfSpfRuns record how many times the intra-area route table was calculated, typically using Dijkstra's algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the status lights. They show whether a neighbor router is just saying hello or is fully caught up with the news.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The only related remark is in the row creation discussion, which allows read-write objects to be implemented as read-only while no standard SNMP security architecture exists. The MIB does include an authentication type per area, ospfAuthType, whose default is 0 (no authentication).
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not talk about locking the panel. It only says a maker may make some dials look-only.
